implementation_notes: Modern C++ has the guard built into the language: a function-local static is initialized on the first execution that reaches its declaration, exactly once even when reached from several threads, so `static Resource& r = open();` is already a correct lazy acquisition - cppreference notes this may be more efficient than the equivalent std::call_once. Use std::once_flag/std::call_once when the acquisition is a statement sequence rather than a single initializer, and std::optional<T> when the resource can be released and re-acquired. The classic POSA3 structure (resource proxy plus acquisition policy plus lifecycle manager) earns its keep only when acquisition must be pluggable or release is part of the design; for a single process-wide value the scoped static accessor is the whole pattern.
pitfalls: A throwing initializer leaves the static uninitialized and the next call retries it - and std::call_once explicitly does not flip the flag when the function throws - so a transiently failing acquisition is re-attempted by later callers with no backoff or record.

Static locals are destroyed at exit in an order that is undefined across translation units, so another static object's destructor can reach a resource that is already destroyed (the dead-reference problem).
A function-local static can never be reset or re-acquired; for a resource that must be closed or refreshed, hold std::optional<T> in an owning object and use emplace()/reset() instead.
Function-local statics in a header-inline function are shared only within one program instance; the same accessor in a DLL/dylib gets its own holder, silently producing one resource per module.

variants.name: Deferred acquisition through std::async
variants.implementation_notes: With launch::deferred the callable is stored and the standard calls the evaluation lazy: it runs in the thread that first performs a non-timed wait on the returned future, and the shared state then caches the result or the exception forever. That makes the future a resource holder whose acquisition is a function call, which is useful when the acquired value is produced on the calling thread but at a time of the caller's choosing. Choose it over the scoped static when several independent holders are needed or when the result (including failure) must be observable by many callers.
pitfalls: A deferred future never runs unless it is waited on: discarding the future silently cancels the acquisition, with no error and no resource.
The evaluation runs in the waiting thread, so the first caller pays the entire acquisition cost - never wait on it inside a latency-critical path.
std::async without an explicit policy uses async|deferred, which is implementation-defined: a plain std::async is not a lazy acquisition at all.

variants.name: std::optional holder with emplace/reset
variants.implementation_notes: std::optional makes the not-yet-acquired state part of the type: an empty optional is the holder before first use, emplace() acquires in place, reset() releases, and has_value()/value() keep the check explicit. Choose it over a scoped static when the resource is re-acquirable (a replaced connection) or owned by an object rather than the process. It is not synchronized: guard shared holders with a mutex or std::call_once exactly as you would a raw pointer.
pitfalls: optional is not synchronized: concurrent first calls can both enter emplace and race - the guard still has to be added.
emplace() on a non-empty optional destroys the previous value first, so replacing a live resource must be sequenced with its users.
optional<T> stores the value inline, so a large handle inflates every holder; store a unique_ptr<T> when the resource is big or move-only.
